I always assumed that sharing my programs according to [The Four Freedoms](https://www.gnu.org/philosophy/free-sw.html) was a way to do good. Recently someone gave me reason to think maybe this is not true.

* Nothing I've written is likely to impact the world in a significant way, so it can't do good for anyone. * People might waste their time testing or reviewing my code. Maybe they had more benevolent things to do with their time that might actually change the world. * Bad code, which I have written plenty of, is likely to set bad examples for less experienced programmers. I may damage their potential to write significant world changing software. * Maybe hoping that others will use my code and comment on it is selfish? Maybe sharing my programs is serving a self imposed delusion that I am capable of doing any social good at all?

I think that covers some of the doubts which emerged during our conversation. What I'm hoping to garner in response is:

* Is sharing programs according to The Four Freedoms demonstrably a social good? Does it impact the world in any beneficial way? * What is your motivation for sharing your own code? Do you ever doubt that your motives are purely benevolent and not self serving (or if that even matters to you)? * What are the duties of a programmer to the users of programs shared according to The Four Freedoms, beyond recognizing those freedoms? Do the users have obligations to the programmer? Should the programmer even question this?

I also invite any other relevant commentary on the subject. Thank you for reading.
Is sharing programs always a social good, or is it sometimes a social ill?

Frankly, the reasons you gave for publishing code being an ill are weak or plainly ridiculous.

Like @VoatAntacid said, the impact is unknowable and even bad code can teach people things. How people spend their time is on their shoulders, not yours, and worrying about it is insecure. Sharing is not a selfish act and neither is taking criticism and feedback, provided you do it with humility and aren't feeding narcissism.

If authors thought the same thing about publishing, the world would be a poorer place.

I think it is always a good idea to publish code that respect the four freedom, and I agree with @toats that the reason you gave are weak. I learned what I know from the net all thanks to GNU related licences and code, even if the code was not functional it gave me a idea of what to look for.

Sharing is caring and the impact even of bad code is unknowable and I learnt a lot also from bad code, so go ahead and keep sharing!
